Using the normal approximation to the binomial distribution, approximate the probability that if $150$ people are picked at random, then $70$ of them will have blood type A. Give your answer to three decimal places.\n\n*Hint: The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $\\Phi(z)$ for the standard normal distribution.*\n\n| $z$ | $\\, 0.04 \\,$ | $\\, 0.05 \\,$ | $\\, 0.06 \\,$ | $\\, 0.07 \\,$ | $\\, 0.08 \\,$ |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| $\\, 0.5 \\,$ | $\\, 0.7054 \\,$ | $\\, 0.7088 \\,$ | $\\, 0.7123 \\,$ | $\\, 0.7157 \\,$ | $\\, 0.7190 \\,$ |\n| $\\, 0.6 \\,$ | $\\, 0.7389 \\,$ | $\\, 0.7422 \\,$ | $\\, 0.7454 \\,$ | $\\, 0.7486 \\,$ | $\\, 0.7517 \\,$ |\n| $\\, 0.7 \\,$ | $\\, 0.7704 \\,$ | $\\, 0.7734 \\,$ | $\\, 0.7764 \\,$ | $\\, 0.7794 \\,$ | $\\, 0.7823 \\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Given a binomial random variable $X \\sim B(n,p)$, if\n\n- $np > 5$, and\n- $n(1-p) > 5$,\n\nwe can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\\mu = np$ and variance\n\n$$\n\\sigma^2 = np(1-p)\n$$\n\nthat is,\n\n$$\nY \\sim N(np, np(1-p))\n$$\n\nHere, we have $n=150$ and $p = 0.44$. Therefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nnp &= 150 \\cdot 0.44 \\\\\n&= 66 \\\\\n&> 5✓ \\\\\nn(1 - p) &= 150 \\cdot (1 - 0.44) \\\\\n&= 84 \\\\\n&> 5.✓\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean\n\n$$\n\\mu = np = (150)(0.44) = 66\n$$\n\nand variance\n\n$$\n\\sigma^2 = np(1-p) = (150)(0.44)(1-0.44) = 36.96\n$$\n\nThat is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y \\sim N(66, 36.96)$.\n\nNow, we can approximate the desired probability\n\n$$\nP(X = 70)\n$$\n\nUsing a continuity correction, we have\n\n$$\nP(X =70) \\approx P(69.5 \\leq Y \\leq 70.5)\n$$\n\nTo compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nP(69.5 \\le Y \\le 70.5) &= P(\\frac{69.5 - 66}{\\sqrt{36.96}} \\le Z \\le \\frac{70.5 - 66}{\\sqrt{36.96}}) \\\\\n&\\approx P(0.58 \\le Z \\le 0.74) \\\\\n&= P(Z \\le 0.74) - P(Z < 0.58) \\\\\n&= P(Z \\le 0.74) - P(Z \\le 0.58) \\\\\n&= Φ(0.74) - Φ(0.58) \\\\\n&= 0.7704 - 0.7190 \\\\\n&= 0.0514\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\nP(X = 70)\\approx 0.051\n$$\n\nNote: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.0528$."} {:db/id 17592186050038} {:db/id 17592186050198} {:db/id 17592186050425} {:db/id 17592186115990 :question/id #uuid "58190d0f-af25-525b-8820-0213217d6f88" :question/math-academy-id "q-95099"} {:db/id 17592186115992 :question/id #uuid "1c656830-cd06-512a-9850-cdb6ac44625c" :question/math-academy-id "q-95746"} {:db/id 17592186115317 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186115146 :question/id #uuid "9019ee77-a971-598c-b5b6-4ef903fd5029" :question/math-academy-id "e-8287"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "91946709-3ca8-5501-be63-336b06f6c305" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186115993 :question/id #uuid "5faab60e-ecea-58c0-a299-eb32601cdfdd" :question/math-academy-id "q-95758"} {:db/id 17592186115994 :question/id #uuid "a5478088-f955-551b-89bd-26be2eb62261" :question/math-academy-id "q-95812"} {:db/id 17592186410433 :question/id #uuid "ad031c31-3240-524a-8691-42d16ca618b6" :question/math-academy-id "q-95813"}] :knowledge-point/title "Using a Normal Approximation to Approximate a Binomial Probability Over an Interval"} {:db/id 17592186115146 :question/id #uuid "9019ee77-a971-598c-b5b6-4ef903fd5029" :question/math-academy-id "e-8287" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186115317 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "91946709-3ca8-5501-be63-336b06f6c305" :knowledge-point/title "Using a Normal Approximation to Approximate a Binomial Probability Over an Interval"}] :question/problem "An archer practices firing an arrow at a target $50$ times. Give your final answer to three decimal places.\n\n*Hint: The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $\\Phi(z)$ for the standard normal distribution.*\n\n| $z$$\\, 0.00 \\,$$\\, 0.01 \\,$$\\, 0.02 \\,$$\\, 1.6 \\,$ $\\, 0.9452 \\,$ $\\, 0.9463 \\,$ $\\, 0.9474 \\,$ $\\, 1.7 \\,$ $\\, 0.9554 \\,$ $\\, 0.9564 \\,$ $\\, 0.9573 \\,$ $\\, 1.8 \\,$ $\\, 0.9641 \\,$ $\\, 0.9649 \\,$ $\\, 0.9656 \\,$ |  | $z$$\\, 0.00 \\,$$\\, 0.01 \\,$$\\, 0.02 \\,$$\\, 3.0 \\,$ $\\, 0.9987 \\,$ $\\, 0.9987 \\,$ $\\, 0.9987 \\,$ $\\, 3.1 \\,$ $\\, 0.9990 \\,$ $\\, 0.9991 \\,$ $\\, 0.9991 \\,$ $\\, 3.2 \\,$ $\\, 0.9993 \\,$ $\\, 0.9993 \\,$ $\\, 0.9994 \\,$ |\n| --- | ---: | ---: |" :question/worked-solution "Given a binomial random variable $X \\sim B(n,p)$, if\n\n- $np > 5$, and\n- $n(1-p) > 5$,\n\nwe can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\\mu = np$ and variance\n\n$$\n\\sigma^2 = np(1-p)\n$$\n\nthat is,\n\n$$\nY \\sim N(np, np(1-p))\n$$\n\nHere, we have $n=50$ and $p = 0.47$. Therefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nnp &= 50 \\cdot 0.47 \\\\\n&= 23.5 \\\\\n&> 5✓ \\\\\nn(1 - p) &= 50 \\cdot (1 - 0.47) \\\\\n&= 26.5 \\\\\n&> 5.✓\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean\n\n$$\n\\mu = np = (50)(0.47) = 23.5\n$$\n\nand variance\n\n$$\n\\sigma^2 = np(1-p) = (50)(0.47)(1-0.47) = 12.455\n$$\n\nThat is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y \\sim N(23.5, 12.455)$.\n\nNow, we can estimate the desired probability $P(29 < X < 35)$. Using a continuity correction, we have\n\n$$\nP(29 < X < 35) = P(30 \\leq X \\leq 34) \\approx P(29.5 \\leq Y \\leq 34.5)\n$$\n\nTo compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nP(29.5 \\le Y < 34.5) &= P(\\frac{29.5 - 23.5}{\\sqrt{12.455}} \\le Z \\le \\frac{34.5 - 23.5}{\\sqrt{12.455}}) \\\\\n&\\approx P(1.70 \\le Z \\le 3.12) \\\\\n&= P(Z \\le 3.12) - P(Z < 1.70) \\\\\n&= P(Z \\le 3.12) - P(Z \\le 1.70) \\\\\n&= Φ(3.12) - Φ(1.70) \\\\\n&= 0.9991 - 0.9554 \\\\\n&= 0.0437\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\nP(29 < X < 35) \\approx 0.044\n$$\n\n**Note:** Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.0436$."} {:db/id 17592186115993 :question/id #uuid :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186116233 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116536 :tutorial/content "Suppose the random variable $X\\sim B(n,p)$ follows a binomial distribution.\n\nThere are certain situations where working with binomial random variables becomes difficult. For example, when the parameter $n$ is large, computing exact probabilities can become problematic due to the large numbers involved.\n\nUnder certain conditions, we can approximate the *discrete* random variable $X$ using a *continuous normal* random variable $Y$, given by\n\n$$\nY \\sim N(\\mu, \\sigma^2)\n$$\n\nwhere $\\mu$ and $\\sigma^2$ are calculated using the formulas for the mean and variance of the binomial random variable $X$:\n\n$$\n\\mu = np, \\qquad \\sigma^2 = np(1-p)\n$$\n\nTo determine whether a given binomial distribution can be approximated using a normal distribution, we use the following rule of thumb:\n\n- $np > 5$, and\n- $n(1-p) > 5$.\n\nTo get a feel for how this works, let's consider a few examples of binomial distributions and their corresponding normal approximations:\n\n- First, consider the case where $n=5$ and $p=0.2$. In this case, it's straightforward to show that\n$\\mu = {\\color{blue}{1}},\\qquad \\sigma^2 = {\\color{red}{0.8}}$,\nand\n$np = 1 < 5,\\qquad n(1-p) = 4 < 5$.\nSince $np < 5$, the normal distribution $N({\\color{blue}{1}},{\\color{red}{0.8}})$ is *not* a good approximation to $B(5, 0.2)$. The diagram below compares the two distributions. The yellow rectangles correspond to the values of the PMF of $B(5, 0.2)$, and the smooth blue curve is the PDF of the corresponding normal distribution.![](images/6a/6a67b3ad65bfedcd25b787ff15e72c575da1215ae47502ff11f97d40de407560.png)\n- Next, we consider the case where $n=5$ and $p=0.5$. In this case, it's straightforward to show that\n$\\mu = {\\color{blue}{2.5}},\\qquad \\sigma^2 = {\\color{red}{1.25}}$,\nand\n$np = n(1-p) = 2.5 < 5$.\nSince $np = n(1-p) < 5$, the normal distribution $N({\\color{blue}{2.5}},{\\color{red}{1.25}})$ is *not* a good approximation to $B(5, 0.5)$.![](images/0a/0a8f2d9ccd78ee885ea3bb8f2f00705f69c520f8ec0588411865399b6ecef046.png)\n- Finally, we consider the case where $n=20$ and $p=0.5$. In this case, it's straightforward to show that\n$\\mu = {\\color{blue}{10}},\\qquad \\sigma^2 = {\\color{red}{5}}$,\nand\n$np = n(1-p) = 10 > 5$.\nSince $np > 5$ and $n(1-p) > 5$, the normal distribution $N({\\color{blue}{10}},{\\color{red}{5}})$ *is* a good approximation to $B(20, 0.5)$.![](images/9e/9efc7df7c423ed2d8d6cc70ef820de3cb235f644567a3fec0d0a0e501042e305.png)\n\nThe fact that we can approximate binomial random variables as normal when $np > 5$ and $n(1-p) > 5$ is a consequence of the so-called **central limit theorem** (or CLT). We'll discuss this in more detail at the end of the lesson." :tutorial/id #uuid "4d16ee6a-2c83-55f2-a37f-2b5264587984" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4970 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid random variable $X \\sim B(50,0.6)$. Let's estimate the value of\n\n$$\nP(X=33)\n$$\n\nusing the normal approximation.\n\nGiven a binomial random variable $X \\sim B(n,p)$, if\n\n- $np > 5$, and\n- $n(1-p) > 5$,\n\nwe can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\\mu = np$ and variance\n\n$$\n\\sigma^2 = np(1-p)\n$$\n\nthat is,\n\n$$\nY \\sim N(np, np(1-p))\n$$\n\nHere, we have $n=50$ and $p = 0.6$. Therefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nnp &= 50 \\cdot 0.6 \\\\\n&= 30 \\\\\n&> 5✓ \\\\\nn(1 - p) &= 50 \\cdot (1 - 0.6) \\\\\n&= 20 \\\\\n&> 5.✓\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean\n\n$$\n\\mu = 50\\cdot0.6 = 30\n$$\n\nand variance\n\n$$\n\\sigma^2 = 50\\cdot0.6\\cdot(1-0.6)=12\n$$\n\nThat is, we can approximate $X$ by\n\n$$\nY \\sim N(30,12)\n$$\n\nNow, since $X$ is discrete and $Y$ is continuous, we need to apply a continuity correction. The required continuity correction in this case is\n\n$$\nP(X = 33) \\approx P(32.5 \\leq Y \\leq 33.5)\n$$\n\nTo compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nP(32.5 \\le Y \\le 33.5) &= P(\\frac{32.5 - 30}{\\sqrt{12}} \\le Z \\le \\frac{33.5 - 30}{\\sqrt{12}}) \\\\\n&\\approx P(0.72 \\le Z \\le 1.01) \\\\\n&= P(Z \\le 1.01) - P(Z < 0.72) \\\\\n&= P(Z \\le 1.01) - P(Z \\le 0.72) \\\\\n&= Φ(1.01) - Φ(0.72)\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nUsing a table of values for the CDF of the standard normal distribution, we find that\n\n$$\n\\Phi(1.01) = 0.8438, \\qquad \\Phi(0.72) = 0.7642\n$$\n\nSo, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nP(32.5 \\le Y \\le 33.5) &= Φ(1.01) - Φ(0.72) \\\\\n&= 0.8438 - 0.7642 \\\\\n&= 0.0796\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\nP(X = 33) \\approx 0.0796\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "22b0d565-b5ca-5c37-9d8a-f8a2c8f83fce" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5618 :tutorial/title "Using the Normal Approximation to the Binomial Distribution"} :step/id #uuid "41a4f348-1e37-5763-9563-f9ba63ffa00a" :step/math-academy-id 34580 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116267}} {:db/id 17592186116267 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116543 :tutorial/content "In the last example, we approximated the binomial random variable\n\n$$\nX \\sim B(50,0.6)\n$$\n\nusing a normal random variable\n\n$$\nY \\sim N(30,12)\n$$\n\nand we arrived at the approximation\n\n$$\nP(X=33) \\approx P(32.5 \\leq Y \\leq 33.5) \\approx 0.0796\n$$\n\nIf you were to use a software package to evaluate this approximation, you might get an answer like\n\n$$\nP(X = 33) \\approx P(32.5 \\leq Y \\leq 33.5) \\approx 0.0791\n$$\n\nNotice that there is a difference of around $0.0005$ between the two answers.\n\nThere is a reason for this discrepancy. When we calculated that\n\n$$\nP(X = 33) \\approx P(32.5 \\leq Y \\leq 33.5) \\approx 0.0796\n$$\n\nwe rounded our $z$-values two decimal places and then used a lookup table to find $\\Phi(z)$ for those rounded values. As a result, we introduced some small rounding errors.\n\nTypically, the rounding errors are small, so we will continue to work with a table of values. However, it's worth bearing this in mind if you're using a software package or calculator to compute $\\Phi(z)$." :tutorial/id #uuid "d460cc56-a34f-5495-874f-19d80c5ad3b9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5619 :tutorial/title "A Note on Rounding Errors"} :step/id #uuid "88da9ae9-0589-5f70-ab03-1c92544b026c" :step/math-academy-id 34581 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116235}} {:db/id 17592186116274 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116546 :tutorial/content "According to the so-called **central limit theorem**, if $X_1, X_2, \\ldots X_n$ are independent and identically distributed (I.I.D) random variables, then\n\n$$\nX = \\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \\approx N(n\\mu, n\\sigma^2)\n$$\n\nwhere $n$ is \"sufficiently large,\" and\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[X_i] = \\mu, \\qquad \\textrm{Var}[X_i] = \\sigma^2\n$$\n\nNow, if $X\\sim B(n,p)$, then $X$ can be thought of as a sum of $n$ I.I.D Bernoulli random variables\n\n$$\nX_i\\sim\\textrm{Bernoulli}(p)\n$$\n\nwhere the PMF of each $X_i$ is given by\n\n$$\n{p,\\begin{vmatrix}x = 1 \\\\ 1 - p,\\end{vmatrix}x = 0; 0, \\mid otherwise\n$$\n\nIt can be shown that\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[X_i] = \\mu = p, \\qquad \\textrm{Var}[X_i] = \\sigma^2 = p(1-p)\n$$\n\nTherefore, by substituting our values of $\\mu$ and $\\sigma^2$ into our normal approximation for $X$, we get\n\n$$\nX \\approx N\\left(np, np(1-p)\\right)\n$$\n\nThe \"sufficiently large\" condition on $n$ is taken care of by stipulating that $np > 5$ and $n(1-p) > 5$:\n\n- When $p\\approx 0.5$, then $n\\approx 10$ is sufficiently large for the normal approximation to be applied.\n- However, if $p$ is closer to zero or one, then the distribution of $X$ is not symmetric, and consequently, we need $n$ to be much larger for the central limit theorem to be valid." :tutorial/id #uuid "9a338343-d2c2-54a6-98b5-5033bebeb652" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6514 :tutorial/title "The Normal Approximation as a Consequence of the Central Limit Theorem"} :step/id #uuid "b9f0c982-62ce-5f5d-9d4d-30e10da26092" :step/math-academy-id 39428}] :activity/title "Normal Approximations of Binomial Distributions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186115440} {:db/id 17592186116233 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116536 :tutorial/content "Suppose the random variable $X\\sim B(n,p)$ follows a binomial distribution.\n\nThere are certain situations where working with binomial random variables becomes difficult. Let's estimate the value of\n\n$$\nP(X=33)\n$$\n\nusing the normal approximation.\n\nGiven a binomial random variable $X \\sim B(n,p)$, if\n\n- $np > 5$, and\n- $n(1-p) > 5$,\n\nwe can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\\mu = np$ and variance\n\n$$\n\\sigma^2 = np(1-p)\n$$\n\nthat is,\n\n$$\nY \\sim N(np, np(1-p))\n$$\n\nHere, we have $n=50$ and $p = 0.6$. Therefore,\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nnp &= 50 \\cdot 0.6 \\\\\n&= 30 \\\\\n&> 5✓ \\\\\nn(1 - p) &= 50 \\cdot (1 - 0.6) \\\\\n&= 20 \\\\\n&> 5.✓\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean\n\n$$\n\\mu = 50\\cdot0.6 = 30\n$$\n\nand variance\n\n$$\n\\sigma^2 = 50\\cdot0.6\\cdot(1-0.6)=12\n$$\n\nThat is, we can approximate $X$ by\n\n$$\nY \\sim N(30,12)\n$$\n\nNow, since $X$ is discrete and $Y$ is continuous, we need to apply a continuity correction. The required continuity correction in this case is\n\n$$\nP(X = 33) \\approx P(32.5 \\leq Y \\leq 33.5)\n$$\n\nTo compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nP(32.5 \\le Y \\le 33.5) &= P(\\frac{32.5 - 30}{\\sqrt{12}} \\le Z \\le \\frac{33.5 - 30}{\\sqrt{12}}) \\\\\n&\\approx P(0.72 \\le Z \\le 1.01) \\\\\n&= P(Z \\le 1.01) - P(Z < 0.72) \\\\\n&= P(Z \\le 1.01) - P(Z \\le 0.72) \\\\\n&= Φ(1.01) - Φ(0.72)\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nUsing a table of values for the CDF of the standard normal distribution, we find that\n\n$$\n\\Phi(1.01) = 0.8438, \\qquad \\Phi(0.72) = 0.7642\n$$\n\nSo, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nP(32.5 \\le Y \\le 33.5) &= Φ(1.01) - Φ(0.72) \\\\\n&= 0.8438 - 0.7642 \\\\\n&= 0.0796\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\nP(X = 33) \\approx 0.0796\n$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "22b0d565-b5ca-5c37-9d8a-f8a2c8f83fce" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5618 :tutorial/title "Using the so-called **central limit theorem**, if $X_1, X_2, \\ldots X_n$ are independent and identically distributed (I.I.D) random variables, then\n\n$$\nX = \\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \\approx N(n\\mu, n\\sigma^2)\n$$\n\nwhere $n$ is \"sufficiently large,\" and\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[X_i] = \\mu, \\qquad \\textrm{Var}[X_i] = \\sigma^2\n$$\n\nNow, if $X\\sim B(n,p)$, then $X$ can be thought of as a sum of $n$ I.I.D Bernoulli random variables\n\n$$\nX_i\\sim\\textrm{Bernoulli}(p)\n$$\n\nwhere the PMF of each $X_i$ is given by\n\n$$\n{p,\\begin{vmatrix}x = 1 \\\\ 1 - p,\\end{vmatrix}x = 0; 0, \\mid otherwise\n$$\n\nIt can be shown that\n\n$$\n\\textrm{E}[X_i] = \\mu = p, \\qquad \\textrm{Var}[X_i] = \\sigma^2 = p(1-p)\n$$\n\nTherefore, by substituting our values of $\\mu$ and $\\sigma^2$ into our normal approximation for $X$, we get\n\n$$\nX \\approx N\\left(np, np(1-p)\\right)\n$$\n\nThe \"sufficiently large\" condition on $n$ is taken care of by stipulating that $np > 5$ and $n(1-p) > 5$:\n\n- When $p\\approx 0.5$, then $n\\approx 10$ is sufficiently large for the normal approximation to be applied.\n- However, if $p$ is closer to zero or one, then the distribution of $X$ is not symmetric, and consequently, we need $n$ to be much larger for the central limit theorem to be valid." :tutorial/id #uuid "9a338343-d2c2-54a6-98b5-5033bebeb652" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6514 Consider the following:\n\n$$\nI = \\int_1^\\infty \\frac{1}{x}\\,\\textrm{d}x\n$$\n\nWe can attempt to work out $I$ by integrating over $x\\in[1,a]$ as usual and taking the limit as $a$ tends to positive infinity. Therefore, the integral $I$ is *divergent*." :tutorial/id #uuid "7dfef442-a6e1-5446-ac2a-c51aafd1f10c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 930 :tutorial/title "Divergent Improper Integrals"} :step/id #uuid :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186055571 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056045 :tutorial/content "Suppose $S$ is a set. The **power set** of $S,$ denoted $\\mathcal{P}(S),$ is the set containing every subset of $S,$ *including* the empty set.\n\nFor example, let's find the power set of the set\n\n$$S = \\{ 1,2,3 \\}.$$\n\nTo do this, we list out all the subsets of $S{:}$\n\n- The subset containing no elements is $\\emptyset.$\n- The subsets containing $1$ element are $\\{ 1 \\},$ $\\{ 2 \\},$ and $\\{ 3 \\}.$\n- The subsets containing $2$ elements are $\\{ 1,2 \\},$ $\\{ 1,3 \\},$ and $\\{ 2,3 \\}.$\n- The subset containing $3$ elements is $S$ itself: $\\{ 1,2,3 \\}.$\n\nNow, let's put all these subsets together as elements of a single set. We get\n\n$$\\mathcal{P}(S) = \\big\\{ \\emptyset, \\{1\\}, \\{2\\}, \\{3\\}, \\{ 1,2 \\}, \\{ 1,3 \\}, \\{ 2,3 \\}, \\{ 1,2,3 \\} \\big\\}.$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "cbbf2155-81d5-52d9-b9c0-2416958838b6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8241 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "cccf59fe-5d64-567d-835c-def5b2fb5c93" :step/math-academy-id 153365 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055572}} {:db/id 17592186055572 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056060 :tutorial/content "Another way to generate all the subsets of $S=\\{ 1,2,3 \\}$ is using a tree diagram. We start off with the empty set $\\{\\}$ and generate additional subsets of $S$ by systematically inserting or excluding elements of $S.$\n\nLet's go through the process.\n\n- Start with the empty set $\\{\\}$ at the root node of our tree. This is the parent node.\n- Draw two branches pointing away from the parent node. The tip of each arrow gives a child node. Label one branch 'No' and the other 'Yes'.\n\n![](images/a4/a4b17d8114cc48cdc858d036b839d766dcb60f3b400a096406479c9daf7afac0.png)\n- We'll now write down a subset of $S$ at each child node:\n\n- At the child node (tip of the arrow) whose branch is labeled 'No,' we write down the parent node's set. $$\\{\\}$$\n- At the child node whose branch is labeled 'Yes,' we create a new set by inserting the *first* element of $S$ into the parent node's set. This gives the following subset of $S{:}$ $$\\{1\\}$$ We now have the following diagram.\n\n![](images/61/61c6c192df26a22cac5dddad6b2692a519da055730fe9738f3173cb38229cf8b.png)\n\nWe repeat the process, setting the subsets found in the previous step as the new parent nodes.\n\n- We start by considering the parent node $\\{\\}{:}$\n\n- At the child node whose branch is labeled 'No', we write down the parent node's set. $$\\{\\}$$\n- At the child node whose branch is labeled 'Yes,' we create a new set by inserting the *second* element of $S$ into the parent node's set. This gives the following subset of $S{:}$ $$\\{2\\}$$ We now have the following diagram.\n\n![](images/6e/6e43b6022b5939b824995936d8ab910b7b3d2e821a6c96be63606245f6e60dbb.png)\n- Then, we consider the parent node $\\{1\\}{:}$\n\n- At the child node whose branch is labeled 'No', we write down the parent node's set. $$\\{1\\}$$\n- At the child node whose branch is labeled 'Yes,' we create a new set by inserting the *second* element of $S$ into the parent node's set. This gives the following subset of $S{:}$ $$\\{1,2\\}$$ We now have the following diagram.\n\n![](images/6f/6f81c80039f14260bdfdb8d55a34820874fe518e076d2718629d4faf385e92d5.png)\n- Finally, we repeat the process for the new parent nodes $\\{\\}, \\{2\\}, \\{1\\},$ and $\\{1,2\\}.$\n\nOur final tree diagram looks as follows.\n\n![](images/12/127ee1187ebf3a2cc498c88326285d5adf5d609cf3276885e8c9d525435133eb.png)\n\nThe final column lists all subsets of $S.$\n\n$$\\emptyset = \\{\\},\\quad \\{1\\},\\quad \\{2\\},\\quad \\{3\\},\\quad \\{ 1,2 \\},\\quad \\{ 1,3 \\},\\quad \\{ 2,3 \\},\\quad \\{ 1,2,3 \\}$$\n\nFinally then, we can write down $\\mathcal P(S){:}$\n\n$$\\mathcal{P}(S) = \\big\\{ \\emptyset, \\{1\\}, \\{2\\}, \\{3\\}, \\{ 1,2 \\}, \\{ 1,3 \\}, \\{ 2,3 \\}, \\{ 1,2,3 \\} \\big\\}.$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7a2897eb-b185-5619-bc49-f2ef12df345a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8511 17592186056046 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a finite set $S$ with cardinality $|S|.$ Then, the cardinality of $\\mathcal P(S)$ is given by\n\n$$\\left|\\mathcal{P}(S)\\right| = 2^{\\left| S \\right|}.$$\n\nIn other words, a finite set with cardinality $|S|$ has $2^{|S|}$ subsets.\n\nFor example, for the set $S = \\{ a,b,c \\},$ we have $|S| = 3,$ and therefore\n\n$$\\left|\\mathcal{P}(S)\\right| = 2^{\\left| S \\right|} = 2^3 = 8.$$\n\nThis tells us that $S$ has $8$ subsets, and consequently, $\\mathcal{P}(S)$ has $8$ elements.\n\n$$\\mathcal{P}(S) = \\big\\{ \\underbrace{\\emptyset}_1, \\underbrace{ \\{a\\}}_2, \\underbrace{ \\{b\\}}_3, \\underbrace{ \\{c\\}}_4, \\underbrace{ \\{ a,b \\}}_5, \\underbrace{ \\{ a,c \\}}_6, \\underbrace{ \\{ b,c \\}}_7, \\underbrace{ \\{ a,b,c \\}}_8 \\big\\}$$\n\nNote the following:\n\n- It's clear from our rule that if $S$ is finite, then $\\mathcal P(S)$ is finite.\n- It can be shown that if $S$ is infinite, then $\\mathcal P(S)$ is also infinite.\n\nWe'll discuss power sets of infinite sets at the end of this lesson and in future lessons." :tutorial/id #uuid :step/content {:db/id 17592186056061 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, our primary focus was on power sets of *finite* sets. The definition of the power set of an *infinite* set mirrors that of finite sets. Namely, it comprises all possible subsets.\n\nAs we already understand, for finite sets, the size of power sets grows exponentially based on the size of the underlying set:\n\n$$\\big| \\mathcal{P}(X) \\big| = 2^{|X|}$$\n\nWhen dealing with power sets of infinite sets, the situation is more intricate.\n\nFor example, let's consider $\\mathbb{R}^2,$ the set containing all points on the Cartesian plane. What are the elements of the power set $\\mathcal P(\\mathbb R^2)?$\n\nAny collection of points on the plane is a subset of $\\mathbb R^2.$ Such subsets can be visualized as black-and-white images on the plane, where points belonging to the subset are drawn in black, and points not belonging to the subset are represented in white.\n\nFor instance, each of the following images gives us a specific element of $\\mathcal{P}(\\mathbb{R}^2){:}$\n\n![](images/bb/bbdb49640183563e0cb137b3c57095edd8b81bceac4dcda1bf3460371df17930.png)\n\nIt follows that any text, be it any or all existing Math Academy lessons, those planned for the future, or any other possible text (finite or infinite), including those not yet written, are all contained within $\\mathcal{P}(\\mathbb{R}^2).$\n\n![](images/c4/c47487cf1a7253bfafd5419cd824df30669a575d4b90f3fddc36566e920325bc.png)\n\nIt's somewhat extraordinary that such a vast and important set can be expressed using just the symbols $\\mathcal P(\\mathbb R^2).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ca3f303c-7c55-5abe-945a-dfe8a4816aa8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8512 :tutorial/title "Power Sets of Infinite Sets"} :step/id #uuid "3f3fd95b-66c4-5c77-81de-9a4ba5c39f8e" :step/math-academy-id 153382}] :activity/title "Power Sets" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186054910} {:db/id 17592186055571 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056045 :tutorial/content "Suppose $S$ is a set. The **power set** of $S,$ denoted $\\mathcal{P}(S),$ is the set containing every subset of $S,$ *including* the empty set.\n\nFor example, let's find the power set of the set\n\n$$S = \\{ 1,2,3 \\}.$$\n\nTo do this, we list out all the subsets of $S{:}$\n\n- The subset containing no elements is $\\emptyset.$\n- The subsets containing $1$ element are $\\{ 1 \\},$ $\\{ 2 \\},$ and $\\{ 3 \\}.$\n- The subsets containing $2$ elements are $\\{ 1,2 \\},$ $\\{ 1,3 \\},$ and $\\{ 2,3 \\}.$\n- The subset containing $3$ elements is $S$ itself: $\\{ 1,2,3 \\}.$\n\nNow, let's put all these subsets together as elements of a single set. We get\n\n$$\\mathcal{P}(S) = \\big\\{ \\emptyset, \\{1\\}, \\{2\\}, \\{3\\}, \\{ 1,2 \\}, \\{ 1,3 \\}, \\{ 2,3 \\}, \\{ 1,2,3 \\} \\big\\}.$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "cbbf2155-81d5-52d9-b9c0-2416958838b6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8241 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "cccf59fe-5d64-567d-835c-def5b2fb5c93" :step/math-academy-id 153365 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055572}} {:db/id 17592186056045 :tutorial/content "Suppose $S$ is a set. We get\n\n$$\\mathcal{P}(S) = \\big\\{ \\emptyset, \\{1\\}, \\{2\\}, \\{3\\}, \\{ 1,2 \\}, \\{ 1,3 \\}, \\{ 2,3 \\}, \\{ 1,2,3 \\} \\big\\}.$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "cbbf2155-81d5-52d9-b9c0-2416958838b6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8241 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186055572 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056060 :tutorial/content "Another way to generate all the subsets of $S=\\{ 1,2,3 \\}$ is using a tree diagram. We start off with the empty set $\\{\\}$ and generate additional subsets of $S$ by systematically inserting or excluding elements of $S.$\n\nLet's go through the process.\n\n- Start with the empty set $\\{\\}$ at the root node of our tree. This is the parent node.\n- Draw two branches pointing away from the parent node. The tip of each arrow gives a child node. The equations of the system define two straight lines, so we can visualize the system by plotting both lines on the same graph.\n\n![](images/ee/ee391c2910264abc2962d0c5ec3d971eb7b0b818b5bd59af33fc16ab9e931d11.png)\n\nThe solution of the system corresponds to the point where the two lines intersect. In this case, it is the point $(2,6)$, as shown above. So $x=2$ and $y=6$ form the **solution** to the system. We can write the solution as the ordered pair $(2, 6)$.\n\nWhenever we find a solution to a system of equations, it is a good idea to double-check our result. To check that the solution $x=2,y=6$ is the correct solution, we substitute our solution into *both* of the equations.\n\nLet's check the first equation.\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nx - y &= -4 \\\\\n(2) - (6) &= -4 \\\\\n- 4 &= -4✓\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow we check the second equation:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\n6x - y &= 6 \\\\\n6(2) - 6 &= 6 \\\\\n6 &= 6✓\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince $x=2$ and $y=6$ satisfied *both* equations, it is indeed the solution to the system of equations." :tutorial/id #uuid "84e2025e-9a3e-50ad-9b6b-dcc75fb2b7c2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8209 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "331a78d4-5c29-520f-a140-cfab1b9cf26b" :step/math-academy-id 196434 :step/next {:db/id 17592186139351}} {:db/id 17592186139351 :step/content {:db/id 17592186138428 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186138083 :question/id #uuid "cbf28a0c-c34d-5855-b72e-4225a11710c1" :question/math-academy-id "e-13129"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0f80bc47-7b56-5357-b4e7-718f4ddfa41b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050790}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186138700} {:db/id 17592186138764}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Solution to a System From Its Graph"} :step/id #uuid "bbbe689a-fd82-54c6-b18a-876c6124c4f7" :step/math-academy-id 196435 :step/next {:db/id 17592186139352}} {:db/id 17592186139352 :step/content {:db/id 17592186138429 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186138084 :question/id #uuid "86771ced-afc0-5061-a532-bc2345a52ea8" :question/math-academy-id "e-13130"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4154d81b-c94a-57f7-80fa-0daa341505e6" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186138783} {:db/id 17592186139116}] :knowledge-point/title "Word Problems"} :step/id #uuid "3a86bd4f-c706-59ab-986e-311feb0009df" :step/math-academy-id 196439}] :activity/title "Introduction to Systems of Linear Equations" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186138586} {:db/id 17592186139350 :step/content {:db/id 17592186139667 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to know the values of $x$ and $y$ that satisfy *both* of the equations\n\n$$\n{x - }_{0}^{1}\\sqrt{x+t}\\,\\text{d}x,\\,t>0$\n\nII. ${F}_{2}(t)={\\int }_{0}^{1}\\frac{xt}{{x}^{2}+{t}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}x,\\,t>0$\n\nIII. ${F}_{3}(t)={\\int }_{0}^{1}\\frac{1}{x-t}\\,\\text{d}x,\\,t>1$\n\nSelect all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Suppose $f(x,t)$ is continuous on $R=[a,b]\\times [c,d]$ and $\\frac{∂f}{∂t}$ exists and is continuous on $R.$ Then, the function\n\n$$\nF(t)={\\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\\,\\text{d}x\n$$\n\nis differentiable on $(c,d),$ and\n\n$$\n{F}^{′}(t)=\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}t}{\\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\\,\\text{d}x={\\int }_{a}^{b}\\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\\,\\text{d}x.\n$$\n\nThis is known as *differentiating under the integral sign.*\n\nWith that in mind, let's check each function:\n\n- For the first function, we have \n\n$$\n{f}_{1}(x,t)=\\sqrt{x+t}.\n$$\n\nWe fix ${t}_{0}>0$ and choose $[c,d]⊂(0,\\infty )$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\\times [c,d].$\n\nNote that ${f}_{1}$ is continuous on $R.$ Computing the partial derivative, we have\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂t}=\\frac{1}{2\\sqrt{x+t}},\n$$\n\nwhich exists and is continuous on $R$ (since $x+t\\ge c>0$ on $R$). Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{1}^{′}(t)$ for all real $t>0.$\n\n- For the second function, we have \n\n$$\n{f}_{2}(x,t)=\\frac{xt}{{x}^{2}+{t}^{2}}.\n$$\n\nWe fix ${t}_{0}>0$ and choose $[c,d]⊂(0,\\infty )$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\\times [c,d].$\n\nNote that ${f}_{2}$ is continuous on $R$ (since the denominator never vanishes on $R$). Computing the partial derivative, we have\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂t}=\\frac{x({x}^{2}+{t}^{2})-2x{t}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+{t}^{2})^{2}},\n$$\n\nwhich exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{2}^{′}(t)$ for all real $t>0.$\n\n- For the third function, we have \n\n$$\n{f}_{3}(x,t)=\\frac{1}{x-t}.\n$$\n\nWe fix ${t}_{0}>1$ and choose $[c,d]⊂(1,\\infty )$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\\times [c,d].$\n\nNote that for $t>1$ and $x\\in [0,1],$ the denominator $x-t$ never vanishes on $R,$ so ${f}_{3}$ is continuous on $R.$ Computing the partial derivative, we have\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂t}=\\frac{1}{(x-t)^{2}},\n$$\n\nwhich exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{3}^{′}(t)$ for all real $t>1.$\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I, II, and III.\""} {:db/id 17592186311551 :question/id #uuid "57d1f543-d099-580f-9280-d60da64177c3" :question/math-academy-id "q-335248" }_{0}^{1}{e}^{-{t}^{2}x}\\,\\text{d}x,\\,t\\in R$\n- **II.** ${F}_{2}(t)={\\int }_{0}^{1}|x-t|\\,\\text{d}x,\\,t\\ge 0$\n- **III.** ${F}_{3}(t)={\\int }_{0}^{1}\\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{t}^{2}}\\,\\text{d}x,\\,t>0$\n\nSelect all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Suppose $f(x,t)$ is continuous on $R=[a,b]\\times [c,d]$ and $\\frac{∂f}{∂t}$ exists and is continuous on $R.$ Then, the function\n\n$$\nF(t)={\\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\\,\\text{d}x\n$$\n\nis differentiable on $(c,d),$ and\n\n$$\n{F}^{′}(t)=\\frac{\\text{d}}{\\text{d}t}{\\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,t)\\,\\text{d}x={\\int }_{a}^{b}\\frac{∂f}{∂t}(x,t)\\,\\text{d}x.\n$$\n\nThis is known as *differentiating under the integral sign.*\n\nWith that in mind, let's check each function:\n\n- For the first function, we have \n\n$$\n{f}_{1}(x,t)={e}^{-{t}^{2}x}.\n$$\n\nWe fix ${t}_{0}\\in R$ and choose $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\\times [c,d].$\n\nNote that ${f}_{1}$ is continuous on $R.$ Computing the partial derivative, we have\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂t}=-2tx{e}^{-{t}^{2}x},\n$$\n\nwhich exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{1}^{′}(t)$ for all real $t.$\n\n- For the second function, we have \n\n$$\n{f}_{2}(x,t)=|x-t|.\n$$\n\nWe fix ${t}_{0}\\in (0,1)$ and choose $c<{t}_{0}<d$ such that $[c,d]⊆[0,1],$ so $R=[0,1]\\times [c,d].$\n\nNote that ${f}_{2}$ is continuous on $R.$ However, the partial derivative\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂t}={\\begin{aligned}-1,\\,x>t \\\\ 1,\\,x<t\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\ndoes *not* exist whenever $x=t={t}_{0},$ and is therefore not defined everywhere on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is *not* valid.\n\n- For the third function, we have \n\n$$\n{f}_{3}(x,t)=\\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{t}^{2}}.\n$$\n\nWe fix ${t}_{0}>0$ and choose $[c,d]⊂(0,\\infty )$ such that $c<{t}_{0}<d,$ so $R=[0,1]\\times [c,d].$\n\nNote that ${f}_{3}$ is continuous on $R$ (since the denominator never vanishes on $R$). Computing the partial derivative, we have\n\n$$\n\\frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂t}=-\\frac{2t}{({x}^{2}+{t}^{2})^{2}},\n$$\n\nwhich exists and is continuous on $R.$ Thus, differentiating under the integral sign is valid at ${t}_{0}.$ And since our choice of ${t}_{0}$ was arbitrary, we can compute ${F}_{3}^{′}(t)$ for all $t>0.$\n\nTherefore, the correct answer is \"I and III only.\""} {:db/id 17592186311556 {:db/id 17592186230110}} {:db/id 17592186230110 :step/content {:db/id 17592186230197 :tutorial/content "Consider the function\n\n$$\nF(t) = \\int_{a}^b f(x,t)\\,\\textrm{d} x, \\qquad t \\in [c,d].\n$$\n\nThen, *differentiation under the integral sign* applies, meaning\n\n$$\nF'(t) = \\int_{a}^b \\frac{\\partial f}{\\partial t}(x,t)\\,\\textrm{d} x,\n$$\n\nprovided the following conditions are met:\n\n- $f(x,t)$ is continuous on $R = [a,b] \\times [c,d],$ and\n\n- $\\dfrac{\\partial f}{\\partial t}$ exists and is continuous on $R.$\n\nFor example, suppose we wish to compute $I'(t),$ where\n\n$$\nI(t)=\\int_{0}^{1} (2x+t^3)^2 \\, \\textrm{d}x, \\qquad t \\in [0,5].\n$$\n\nWe may differentiate under the integral sign provided that the function $f(x,t) = (2x+t^3)^2$ fits =-4t(3x-{t}^{2}).\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSubstituting this back into our integral, we get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(t) & ={\\int }_{-1}^{1}-4t(3x-{t}^{2})\\,\\text{d}x \\\\  & =-4t{\\int }_{-1}^{1}(3x-{t}^{2})\\,\\text{d}x.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, let's evaluate the remaining integral:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\int }_{-1}^{1}(3x-{t}^{2})\\,\\text{d}x & ={\\int 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1005 17592186046967 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1007 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II" 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II continues the development of advanced mathematical techniques used throughout modern physics. Building on the analytical framework established in the first course, students study orthogonality, multivariable integration, vector calculus theorems, and advanced methods for differential equations.\nThe course emphasizes mathematical structures that arise naturally in physics, including inner product spaces, orthogonal projections, integral theorems of vector calculus, and transform methods for solving differential equations. These tools provide the mathematical foundation for analyzing electromagnetic fields, wave phenomena, dynamical systems, and statistical models encountered in advanced physics courses." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1009 "The course begins with the theory of projections in inner product spaces. Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.\nStudents then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.\nApplications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.\nThe course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.\nStudents next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.\nApplications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.\nThe course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.\nLaplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.\nThe course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics. Students analyze the accuracy and stability of numerical schemes used in computational physics and study multivariate probability distributions and the central limit theorem, which appear in statistical physics and experimental analysis." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1012 155 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1013 "PS2" 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1014 #uuid [17592186046658 1005 17592186046975 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1007 "Mathematics for Machine Learning" 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1008 "Our Mathematics for Machine Learning course provides a comprehensive foundation of the essential mathematical tools required to study modern machine learning.\nThis course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.\nOn completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.\nStudents then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.\nAs part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.\nStudents will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data.\nThe course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data.\nA solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks.\nStudents also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.\nStudents work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.\nOn the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.\nStudents extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.\nThe course concludes with parametric inference, focusing on point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals, which form the statistical foundation for many machine learning methods." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1012 145 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I" 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I develops the core mathematical structures and analytical tools used throughout theoretical and applied physics. Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.\nStudents learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.\nStudents then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.\nThe course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.\nThe course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.\nStudents then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.\nThe final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. The course concludes with second-order linear differential equations and oscillatory systems, including harmonic motion, damped oscillators, and resonance—fundamental mathematical models for vibrating strings, mechanical systems, and electromagnetic circuits." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1012 154 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1013 "PS1" 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1014 #uuid In the undamped model, this causes the oscillations to grow larger and larger over time.\n\nIn the ideal undamped model, resonance produces a particular solution that grows in magnitude with time (due to the extra factor of $t$). This is why the model predicts that the amplitude increases *without bound*.\n\nFor example, consider the undamped forced oscillator\n\n$$\ny'' + 9y = \\sin(3t).\n$$\n\nThe complementary solution is of the form $y_c = A\\cos(3t) + B\\sin(3t),$ the natural frequency of the system is $\\omega = 3,$ and the forcing frequency is also $3.$ Because these frequencies match, resonance occurs.\n\nSince the forcing term $\\sin(3t)$ duplicates a term in the homogeneous solution, we must multiply our guess by $t.$ We try a solution of the form $y_p = t(C\\cos(3t) + D\\sin(3t)).$\n\nCalculating the derivatives of $y_p,$ substituting them into the equation, and equating coefficients of $\\sin(3t)$ and $\\cos(3t)$ yields $C=-\\dfrac16$ and $D=0.$ So, the particular solution is of the form\n\n$$\ny_p = -\\dfrac{t}{6}\\cos(3t).\n$$\n\nNotice that this solution grows larger as $t$ increases. This time-dependent growth illustrates how resonance leads to an increase in oscillation amplitude in the undamped model.\n\nIn real systems, perfectly *unbounded growth* does not occur because physical effects, such as damping and energy loss, eventually limit the amplitude.
